leads.text: Attacker-controlled regex pattern reaches new RegExp() and is executed against run text with no validation, enabling ReDoS (Regular Expression Denial of Service). Chain: POST /v1/checklists (packages/backend/src/api/v1/checklists.ts, checklists.post('/')) stores `data: FilterLogic` from ctx.request.body verbatim into the `checklist.data` column with zero schema validation (comment literally says 'TODO: full zod'). A checklist entry can be `{id:'regex', params:{regex:'<attacker pattern>', field:'output', type:'contains'}}`. Later, POST /v1/evaluations/run (packages/backend/src/api/v1/evaluations/index.ts, evaluations.post('/run')) reads that checklist's `data` as `checks`, builds `virtualRun` directly from the SAME request body's `input`/`output` fields, and calls `runChecksOnRun(virtualRun, checks)` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/evaluations/utils.ts:81, confirmed reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1). Because the 'regex' check has an `evaluator` (not `.sql`), `hasNonSQLFilter` routes it through `checkRun` -> `runner.evaluator!(run, params)` (packages/backend/src/checks/runChecks.ts:98) which dispatches to the CHECK_RUNNERS 'regex' entry in packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts: `const re = new RegExp(regex); const has = re.test(lastMsg(run[field]))`. Both the evil regex AND the text it's matched against (`output`/`input`) are fully attacker-controlled in a single request, so a catastrophic-backtracking pattern (e.g. `(a+)+$`) with a crafted non-matching string will hang the Node.js event loop. A second, independently-confirmed trigger path exists via POST /v1/radars (packages/backend/src/api/v1/radars.ts, radars.post('/')) which stores `checks: any[]` equally unvalidated into `radar.checks`; the background job packages/backend/src/jobs/radar.ts (`runRadarChecksOnRun`) later calls `runChecksOnRun(run, checks, true)` (line 12, reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1) which reaches the exact same `new RegExp(regex)` call (uid 3659ddc82e888cddad2a6d02f4f1412c3809d923, reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1) against real logged run data.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts' AND c.code CONTAINS 'RegExp' RETURN ... -> returned 'const re = new RegExp(regex)' at line 100, reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1. Semantic search + direct CpgCall queries on checklists.ts/evaluations/index.ts/radars.ts/radar.ts confirmed the full source->sink chain: checklists.post('/') stores unvalidated FilterLogic body (`const { slug, type, data } = ctx.request.body`), evaluations.post('/run') pulls `checks = checklistData.data` and calls runChecksOnRun(virtualRun, checks) built from the same request's input/output; runChecksOnRun (packages/backend/src/checks/runChecks.ts, hasNonSQLFilter/checkRun logic queried directly) dispatches non-SQL checks to `runner.evaluator!(run, params)`; CHECK_RUNNERS 'regex' entry code: `evaluator: async (run, params) => { const { regex, type, field } = params; const re = new RegExp(regex); const has = re.test(lastMsg(run[field])); ... }`. radars.post('/') code: `const { description, view, checks, alerts, negative } = ctx.request.body as {...}` then `insert into radar ... checks: sql.json(checks)` with no validation; radar.ts: `const checks: FilterLogic = radar.checks; const { passed, results } = await runChecksOnRun(run, checks, true)` (reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1).

leads.text: Attacker-controlled filter value is interpolated directly inside hard-coded single quotes within a postgres.js tagged-template SQL fragment instead of being passed as a bound value or nested sql fragment, in the 'date' CHECK_RUNNERS entry: `sql\`created_at ${postgresOperators(operator)} '${date}'\`` (packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts, CHECK_RUNNERS id 'date'). `date` comes from `params.date`, which is attacker-controlled FilterLogic supplied via the querystring of GET /v1/runs (packages/backend/src/api/v1/runs/index.ts: `const deserializedFilters = deserializeLogic(queryString); const filtersQuery = ... convertChecksToSQL(deserializedFilters) ...`), which calls `runner.sql(logicElement.params)` for each filter node (packages/backend/src/utils/filters.ts). Because `date` is placed inside literal quote characters in the raw template text rather than passed as a plain parameter or via `sql()`/nested sql-fragment composition (as every other safe CHECK_RUNNERS entry does, e.g. `sql\`status = ${status}\``), this is at minimum a functional bug that could corrupt the generated query, and should be checked by a SQL-driver-aware reviewer for whether the quoting can be abused to break out of the intended value context (classic single-quote SQL injection pattern) depending on exactly how the `sql` tagged-template library (postgres.js, imported from '@/src/utils/db') resolves a bare `${value}` placed between literal quote characters in the template text.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts' AND c.name='sql' RETURN c.code,c.line -> returned `sql`created_at ${postgresOperators(operator)} '${date}'`` at line 222 (CHECK_RUNNERS id 'date', params destructured as `{operator, date}`), contrasted with every sibling entry (e.g. line 86 `status = ${status}`, line 76 `type = ${type}`) which interpolate the raw value WITHOUT surrounding literal quotes. Semantic search on packages/backend/src/api/v1/runs/index.ts confirmed: `const queryString = ctx.querystring; const deserializedFilters = deserializeLogic(queryString); const filtersQuery = ... convertChecksToSQL(deserializedFilters) ...`, and packages/backend/src/utils/filters.ts confirmed `return runner.sql(logicElement.params)` is called with attacker-supplied params for each filter.

leads.text: Koa CORS middleware (patchedCors / @koa/cors config) reflects the request's Origin header back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin ('ctx.get("Origin") || "*"') while also setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The expected control here -- a fixed allow-list of trusted origins -- is absent; any third-party site can issue credentialed cross-origin requests (with the caller's bearer token/cookies) and read the response, defeating the same-origin policy for the whole API.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.scan_id=$scan_id AND c.file_path='packages/backend/src/utils/cors.ts' RETURN c.code,c.line -- returned patchedCors (line 5): 'ctx.set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", ctx.get("Origin") || "*")' + 'ctx.set("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials","true")' (lines 7/9), and the @koa/cors call (line 17) with 'origin(ctx){ return ctx.get("Origin") || "*" }, credentials: true'. A follow-up query for helmet/CSP/X-Frame-Options/csrf across the whole scan returned 0 rows, confirming no origin allow-list or other compensating header control exists anywhere in the codebase.

leads.text: projects.patch('/:projectId') updates the project's name using only the :projectId URL param, with no check that the project belongs to the caller's ctx.state.orgId. Any authenticated user from any org can rename an arbitrary other org's project just by guessing/enumerating a project id.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/projects/index.ts calls named patch/delete/get/post returned: 'projects.patch("/:projectId", async (ctx: Context) => { const { projectId } = ctx.params ... update project set name = ${name} where id = ${projectId} })' -- no org_id predicate in the UPDATE and ctx.state.orgId is never read in this handler, unlike the sibling projects.post('/') handler in the same file which always scopes inserts to ctx.state.orgId.

leads.text: projects.delete('/:projectId') only checks that the CALLER's own org (ctx.state.orgId) has more than one project before deleting; it never verifies that the target :projectId actually belongs to ctx.state.orgId. A user in Org A with >1 project can delete any other org's project by supplying its id.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/projects/index.ts returned: 'projects.delete("/:projectId", async (ctx) => { const { projectId } = ctx.params; const { orgId } = ctx.state; const [{count}] = await sql`select count(*)::int from project where org_id = ${orgId}`; if (count>1) { await sql`delete from project where id = ${projectId}` } })' -- the DELETE statement filters only by id, never by org_id, so the count check guards the wrong row set.

leads.text: versions.patch('/:id') (template_version) updates content/extra/testValues/isDraft for an arbitrary template_version id with no project ownership check at all -- unlike templates.patch('/:id') and templates.delete('/:id') in the sibling file which both filter by 'project_id = ${ctx.state.projectId}'. Any authenticated caller can overwrite any other project's prompt template content by id.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/templateVersions.ts returned: 'versions.patch("/:id", async (ctx) => { const {content,extra,testValues,isDraft} = ctx.request.body; ... update template_version set content=..., extra=..., test_values=..., is_draft=... where id = ${ctx.params.id} returning * })' -- ctx.state.projectId is never referenced in this handler.

leads.text: versions.get('/:id') (template_version) fetches the full template_version row by id BEFORE any ownership check, then separately queries 'template where project_id = ... and id = version.templateId' only to attach a (possibly undefined) 'template' field. The version's own content/extra is placed in ctx.body regardless of whether the ownership query matched, so a caller from a different project still receives the full template_version content (an authorization bypass via incomplete check), and if the ownership query returns nothing the code additionally throws on 'version.extra' uncamel on an undefined row only in the no-row case -- in the row-exists case content leaks unconditionally.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/templateVersions.ts returned: 'versions.get("/:id", async (ctx) => { const [version] = await sql`select * from template_version where id = ${ctx.params.id}`; version.extra = unCamelObject(version.extra); const [template] = await sql`select * from template where project_id = ${ctx.state.projectId} and id = ${version.templateId}`; ctx.body = { ...version, template } })' -- the first select is unscoped by project.

leads.text: templates.post('/:id/versions') inserts a new template_version row with template_id = ctx.params.id taken directly from the URL, with no check that this template belongs to ctx.state.projectId -- unlike templates.get/patch/delete('/:id') in the same file which all filter by 'project_id = ${ctx.state.projectId}'. Any authenticated user can add arbitrary version content to any other project's template by guessing its id.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/templates.ts returned: 'templates.post("/:id/versions", async (ctx) => { const {content,extra,testValues,isDraft} = ctx.request.body; const [templateVersion] = await sql`insert into template_version (template_id, content, extra, test_values, is_draft) values (${ctx.params.id}, ...)` })' with no reference to ctx.state.projectId, contrasted with templates.get("/:id") in the same file which does 'where project_id = ${ctx.state.projectId} and id = ${ctx.params.id}'.

leads.text: datasets.delete('/:id') deletes a dataset by id with no project ownership check at all, while the PATCH handler for the exact same route pattern (defined immediately above it in the same file) correctly scopes its UPDATE with 'and project_id = ${projectId}'. Any authenticated user (any valid project/org bearer token) can delete another project's dataset by id.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/datasets/index.ts returned: 'datasets.patch("/:id", ...) update dataset set slug = ${slug} where id = ${id} and project_id = ${projectId}' (line 96) immediately followed by 'datasets.delete("/:id", async (ctx) => { const {id} = ctx.params; await sql`delete from dataset where id = ${id}`; ctx.status = 200 })' (line 111) which omits projectId entirely.

leads.text: All dataset-prompt and dataset-variation sub-resource routes (GET/PATCH/DELETE /prompts/:id, GET/DELETE /variations/:id, PATCH /variations/:variationId) operate purely on the URL id with no join/filter back to ctx.state.projectId, so any authenticated caller can read, modify or delete another project's prompt/variation rows by id -- contrast with the project-scoped dataset list/create routes ('datasets.get("/")', 'datasets.post("/")') in the same file.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/datasets/index.ts (lines 111-260) returned, e.g.: 'datasets.get("/prompts/:id", ...) select * from dataset_prompt where id = ${id}' (149), 'datasets.delete("/prompts/:id", ...) delete from dataset_prompt where id = ${id}' (166), 'datasets.patch("/prompts/:id", ...) update dataset_prompt set messages = ${messages} where id = ${id}' (176), 'datasets.get("/variations/:id", ...) select * from dataset_prompt_variation where id = ${id}' (188), 'datasets.delete("/variations/:id", ...) delete from dataset_prompt_variation where id = ${id}' (202), 'datasets.patch("/variations/:variationId", ...) update dataset_prompt_variation set ... where id = ${variationId}' (211) -- none reference projectId.

leads.text: evaluations.get('/result/:evaluationId') returns all evaluation_result rows (joined with prompt/variation content) for an arbitrary evaluationId with no project ownership check, unlike the sibling evaluations.get('/:id') route in the same file which filters by 'and project_id = ${projectId}'. Any authenticated caller can read another project's evaluation results (including prompt content) by guessing the evaluation id.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/evaluations/index.ts returned: 'evaluations.get("/result/:evaluationId", async (ctx) => { const {evaluationId} = ctx.params; const results = await sql`select *, p.id as prompt_id, p.messages as prompt_content from evaluation_result er left join dataset_prompt p ... where er.evaluation_id = ${evaluationId}`; ctx.body = results })' (line 72) -- ctx.state.projectId is never read, contrasted with 'evaluations.get("/:id")' (line 57) in the same file which does 'where id = ${id} and project_id = ${projectId}'.

leads.text: external-users GET '/:id' returns a full external_user row by id with no org/project ownership filter, unlike the sibling list route 'users.get("/")' in the same file which scopes by ctx.state.projectId. Any authenticated caller from any project can fetch another project's end-user PII (name/email/etc.) by guessing an external_user id.
leads.evidence: Query on packages/backend/src/api/v1/external-users.ts returned: 'users.get("/:id", async (ctx) => { const {id} = ctx.params; const [row] = await sql`select * from external_user where id = ${id} limit 1`; ctx.body = row })' (line 70) with no reference to ctx.state.projectId, versus 'users.get("/")' (line 9) in the same file which begins 'const { projectId } = ctx.state'.

leads.text: No security-headers middleware (helmet, Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, etc.) is present anywhere in the backend -- the only header-setting code found is the CORS middleware. For an API that also redirects browsers (e.g. ctx.redirect to NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL in the email-verification route) and serves JSON that could be rendered, the absence of these baseline response-hardening headers is a missing control across the whole app.
leads.evidence: Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall) WHERE c.scan_id=$scan_id AND (c.code CONTAINS 'helmet' OR c.code CONTAINS 'X-Frame' OR c.code CONTAINS 'Content-Security-Policy' OR c.code CONTAINS 'csrf' OR c.code CONTAINS 'csurf' OR c.code CONTAINS 'CSRF') -- returned 0 rows across the entire scan_id. The only ctx.set(...) header calls found anywhere were the CORS headers in utils/cors.ts.

leads.text: In authMiddleware (packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/utils.ts), a bearer token on a 'public' route is first checked against validateUUID() before being trusted as ctx.state.projectId (lines 89-93), but immediately below it a second, redundant `if (isPublicRoute)` block (lines 95-102) re-extracts the same bearer token and sets ctx.state.projectId = bearerToken whenever it is merely `typeof bearerToken === 'string'` -- with no UUID/format validation at all. Any request to a public route (matched via the publicRoutes list, e.g. the regexes `/v1/datasets/.+`, `/v1/runs/.+/public`, `/v1/runs/.+/feedback`, or string routes like `/v1/runs/ingest`, `/v1/template_versions/latest`) whose Authorization header is a non-UUID string falls through the first guard (since `!bearerToken` is false and `validateUUID(bearerToken)` is false) and lands in the second block, which accepts the raw token as the project scope unchecked. This looks like a validation fix (the UUID check) that was added in one branch while the old, unguarded code path was left intact directly beneath it -- a classic half-reverted protection. Downstream handlers (e.g. packages/backend/src/api/v1/templates.ts, templateVersions.ts) use ctx.state.projectId directly as the tenant-scoping key in SQL queries, so an attacker who can reach any publicRoutes-matched path can set projectId to an arbitrary string and potentially access/mutate data belonging to another project/org.
leads.evidence: run_cypher on CpgCall uid 873670ab77ce172ae840f5339609d79f7a63bfea (file packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/utils.ts, line 81) returned the full authMiddleware body: `const isPublicRoute = publicRoutes.some(...)`; `if (isPublicRoute && (!bearerToken || validateUUID(bearerToken))) { if (validateUUID(bearerToken)) { ctx.state.projectId = bearerToken } ... }` followed immediately by `if (isPublicRoute) { const bearerToken = ...; if (typeof bearerToken === 'string') { ctx.state.projectId = bearerToken } await next(); return }`. Cross-checked validateUUID in packages/backend/src/utils/misc.ts (line 20): `function validateUUID(string) { if (!string) return false; const uuidSchema = z.string().uuid(); return uuidSchema.safeParse(string).success }` -- confirming the first branch is a real format check that the second branch skips. Also confirmed via query that ctx.state.projectId is used as a raw tenant-scoping parameter in packages/backend/src/api/v1/templates.ts and templateVersions.ts SQL queries (e.g. `where project_id = ${ctx.state.projectId}`).

leads.text: Email-ownership verification can be fully disabled via the `SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY` environment flag: in the `/auth/signup` handler (packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/index.ts, line 62) a newly-created account's `verified` field is set from `process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY ? true : false`, and `sendVerifyEmail` (packages/backend/src/utils/emails.ts, line 9-10) early-returns without sending any verification email whenever the same flag is set: `if (process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY) { return }`. If this flag is left set (e.g. carried over from a dev/test environment into production), every new signup is marked verified without ever proving control of the email address, undermining the email-verification control. Confidence is lower because the only enforcement of `verified` found in this sweep is a frontend UI nag banner (packages/frontend/components/Layout/Navbar.tsx), not a hard backend authorization gate, so the blast radius of this bypass is unclear without deeper access-control analysis.
leads.evidence: run_cypher keyword sweep matched CpgCall uid 32f9690e0f36154dafcf95295dbbf1997021402e (`_tmp_16.verified = process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY ? true : false`, packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/index.ts line 62) and uid 24c9e4d1c0d4a8f7000e3d605256533f7869f06c (`sendVerifyEmail` function, packages/backend/src/utils/emails.ts line 9: `if (process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY) { return }`). Follow-up query on 'verified' usage across the codebase (packages/backend/src/api/v1/users.ts, packages/frontend/components/Layout/Navbar.tsx) found it is read back only for a UI banner (`user && !user?.verified && (...Verify your email...)`), with no backend route found in this sweep that blocks unverified accounts from using the API.

leads.text: In the LLM-run 'checks' evaluation engine, the 'regex' check type builds a RegExp directly from a fully attacker-supplied pattern string (params.regex) with no validation, size limit, or safe-regex guard, then runs it with .test()/.match() against run message content inside the reachable EntryPoint method `evaluator` (packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts). Because the attacker controls the ENTIRE pattern (not just a fixed literal), they can submit a catastrophic-backtracking pattern (e.g. `(a+)+$`) as a saved check/radar filter and trigger a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) that blocks the Node.js event loop whenever that check runs against any matching run text -- and since these checks can be persisted as recurring 'Radar' jobs (packages/backend/src/jobs/radar.ts calls runRadarChecksOnRun -> runChecksOnRun -> evaluator), the DoS can repeat automatically against the whole dataset.
leads.evidence: Query 1: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'RegExp' OR c.name IN ['match','test','replace','search','split','exec'] ... -> returned the CHECK_RUNNERS 'regex' evaluator block at packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts:70-106 containing `const { regex, type, field } = params; const re = new RegExp(regex); const has = re.test(lastMsg(run[field])); ... run[field].match(re)[0]`, all with reachable_from_entry=true. Query 2: MATCH (m:CpgMethod)-[:CONTAINS_CALL]->(c:CpgCall) WHERE c.file_path='packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts' AND c.line IN [100,102,106,...] -> confirms these calls (uids ce42c810..., 3659ddc8..., 77c57cad..., 68f8b095...) all belong to method `packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts::program:evaluator` at line 471. Query 3: MATCH (e:EntryPoint)-[:ENTERS_AT]->(m:CpgMethod) -> confirms `packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts::program:evaluator` (line 471) is itself an EntryPoint of kind 'handler', exposure 'reachable', meaning its parameters (including `params`/`params.regex`) are untrusted input per the scan's convention. Query 4: MATCH (src:CpgCall)-[f:FLOWS_TO]->(dst:CpgCall) WHERE dst.uid='3659ddc82e888cddad2a6d02f4f1412c3809d923' OR src.uid='3659ddc82e888cddad2a6d02f4f1412c3809d923' -> returned a FLOWS_TO SELF-LOOP on `new RegExp(regex)` (src.uid == dst.uid == 3659ddc8...), confirming this call's own argument is tainted, exactly matching the scan's documented 'attacker-controlled source' signal. Query 5: hop_distance/centrality check -> method `evaluator` has hop_distance=0 (is an entry method), and the `new RegExp(regex)`/`re.test(...)`/`run[field].match(re)` calls all have hop_distance=1, reachable_from_entry=true -- i.e. directly one hop from attacker-controlled entry, not buried deep in the graph. Query 6 (CandidateFlow sink_category enumeration) showed only code_exec/sql/redirect precomputed categories, confirming this ReDoS path is NOT covered by the precomputed CandidateFlow sinks and must be caught by this literal/pattern-focused sweep. I also separately enumerated every regex literal in the codebase (MATCH c.code CONTAINS 'RegExp(' plus the name-based sweep above) and inspected each for nested-quantifier shapes (e.g. /\s+/, /[^a-zA-Z ]/g, /{{(.*?)}}/g, /auth/.+, /{.*?}/gs, etc.) -- none contain a catastrophic nested-quantifier shape like (a+)+; the only real danger is this fully-dynamic, attacker-supplied pattern.
